fullText:
a few thoughts:

1. pretraining science is kind of like how people built quite good steam engines before they understood thermodynamics. “Science owes more to the steam engine than the steam engine owes to science.”-(L.J. Henderson). if nick is right, which i am pretty sure he is, progress points in the direction of more interpretability, and pretraining was "slouching towards monosemanticity". my guess would be that major breakthroughs in interp also advance capabilities

2. nick is a good friend of mine, safe to say my origin story at openai wouldn't have happened if i hadn't met him, and it's fascinating watching him operate and seeing the early drafts evolve into this. he's the most profoundly happy guy I know- not driven by guilt, activism, or religious terror, but by fascination. he of course understands the stakes of understanding neural networks, but it doesn't seem like the core reason he does it: he just loves the neural nets. afaict he's posting this from some beautiful hideaway in tokyo. there's a lesson in there for all the +EV maxers. i feel very grateful to have met him

3. i do think it's crazy how few people across the world were staring at neural nets growing: most have moved to a different level of behaviorist analysis, thinking about reward functions and test scores and whatnot. it does not bode that well for the major model companies, oai included, that fundamental breakthroughs like this are coming from outside. we've become too much of a pressure cooker focusing on local incentives, studying narrow tracks under old paradigms, mostly doing engineering, rather than fundamental research, and implicitly hoping the next model will figure it out

fullText:
Fascinating paper from Google DeepMind.

They studied a market where AI agents bid to answer each user prompt.

Each agent bids its expected reward minus its inference cost. A first-price auction is simple to run, but bidders shade their bids, so a prompt can go to an agent that would not have produced the most value.

The paper shows two features of agent markets that keep this loss small. When several agents value a prompt close to the best one, for example because strong models are distilled into cheaper ones, competition limits the loss. When values mostly depend on how hard the prompt is, efficiency approaches 1 - 1/e^2 of optimal, well above the general bound of 1 - 1/e.

They find that simulations on the EmbedLLM routing dataset match the theory.

https://t.co/7cLDnMozvy
